label: pr-mamou-mani-fit
topic: Client fit for a materials-R&D pilot with the London practice Mamou-Mani and its fabrication arm Fab.Pub: current work, fire rules for interior and temporary pieces, public budget anchors, how small R&D contracts are staged, and a one-page contract skeleton
summary:
Partner name: the brief says "Mamu Money"; I read it as Mamou-Mani (London). The user has NOT confirmed that reading. Nobody was contacted.

What I added today (24 public pages downloaded; 39 of 39 evidence quotes verbatim against saved page text; the check fails when a false quote is injected):

1. Current work. The Tate Modern Turbine Hall piece is live ("Open until 11 April 2027"), and the practice compounded natural powders into PLA and PETG in its own workshop for it. The Hermes Beijing facade is dated 2024-2026 and marked built. The Fortnum & Mason awards (2022-2026) now use reprocessed print waste. Projects not in the earlier record: The Wavery bar at Fortnum & Mason (2023, PLA, made at Fab.Pub), AZ Factory Retail Corners (2021, concept), The Grading Building (2021-2024, design study for Therme Group), a private-house staircase (2024), Casa Angeles (2020, concept), Rive Gauche (2016).

2. Fire rules: the most useful new point. In the England guidance, a plastic wall or ceiling lining gets no easier route. The thermoplastic TP(a)/TP(b) route covers only windows, rooflights, lighting diffusers and suspended ceilings, so a printed PLA lining must meet the normal lining table (C-s3, d2 in ordinary rooms). A structure up for 28 days or less is exempt from the Building Regulations, but the Fire Safety Order's risk assessment still applies to "any place". Fab.Pub publishes a flame-retardant blend name but no class.

3. Budget anchors (other people's public budgets, not the practice's fees). Two London Festival of Architecture 2026 commissions: GBP 36,000 + VAT (up to three months on site, 12.5 % design fee, 10 % minimum contingency) and GBP 50,000 + VAT (design, fabrication, install, removal). Fab.Pub's form: minimum GBP 250, minimum 2 weeks. No Mamou-Mani project budget was found on any page.

4. Contract structure. I found NO public example of a materials-R&D contract between an outside team and an architecture practice. The nearest public templates are UK government R&D procurement (stage-gated, supplier keeps IP) and the Lambert university-business model agreements. The skeleton borrows their shape; that is my inference.

5. Deliverable: D:/Users/ashenoy00000/delphi-work/agents5/pr-mamou-mani-fit/contract-skeleton.md. Three fixed-price phases with go/no-go gates: (1) paper and Formlabs-coupon feasibility, 4-6 weeks; (2) prototype in the client's own blend, 8-12 weeks; (3) installation-ready evidence pack, 8-12 weeks. It has 11 pass/fail acceptance tests and a list of what is not promised (no fire class, no outdoor or structural use, no building energy claim, no service life beyond cycles run).

What was wrong or weak:
- Phase lengths and IP terms in the skeleton are my proposal, not sourced. No price is quoted.
- The 170-cycle and small-flame (150 mm in 60 s) thresholds come from earlier agent records, not pages I re-opened; the earlier fire record itself warned its numbers came through a summariser.
- The skeleton is not tied to the specific linker-biology material: I did not read that proposal, so the element is described generically as moisture-responsive.
- I did not open any temporary-structures guidance beyond the two statutory instruments.
- Budgets and timelines for the practice's own projects are not public on the pages read.

findings.claim: England, Building Regulations 2010, Schedule 2, Class 4: a building up for 28 days or less is exempt from the Building Regulations.

findings.claim: The Fire Safety Order still applies to a short-lived installation: its definition of premises is very wide, and the responsible person must do a fire risk assessment. So exemption from the Building Regulations does not remove fire duties. (The link between the two is my reading, not a quoted sentence.)
findings.evidence_quote: must make a suitable and sufficient assessment of the risks

findings.claim: Approved Document B Volume 2, Table 6.1: linings in ordinary non-small rooms should be class C-s3, d2 (re-read from the PDF today; confirms the earlier fire record).
findings.evidence_quote: Other rooms (including garages) C-s3, d2

findings.claim: NEW: thermoplastics that miss the lining table may only be used as described in paragraphs 6.14-6.18 (windows, rooflights, lighting diffusers, suspended ceilings). There is no European-test route for those uses. A printed PLA wall or ceiling lining therefore has to meet Table 6.1 or fit the partial-area allowance.
findings.evidence_quote: No guidance for European fire test performance is currently available

findings.claim: NEW: a thermoplastic lining is not credited with protecting what is behind it; both the plastic and the substrate must meet the class unless fully bonded to a non-thermoplastic substrate.
findings.evidence_quote: cannot be assumed to protect a substrate

findings.claim: NEW: the TP(b) thermoplastic class has a simple burn-rate threshold on a 1.5-3 mm specimen (BS 2782-0 Method 508A). This is a cheap screening number for a diffuser-type piece, not for a lining.
findings.evidence_quote: have a maximum rate of burning of 50mm/minute

key_claims: The partner name in the brief is still unconfirmed; this work assumes it means the London practice Mamou-Mani.
The practice already compounds its own filled PLA/PETG blends and has a named flame-retardant blend with no published class, so the sellable gap is measured evidence and checked design rules.

A printed plastic wall or ceiling lining in England gets no easier fire route: it must meet the ordinary lining class (C-s3, d2 in ordinary rooms); the thermoplastic route covers only windows, rooflights, diffusers and suspended ceilings.
A structure up for 28 days or less is exempt from the Building Regulations, but a fire risk assessment under the Fire Safety Order is still required.
Public London installation commissions in 2026 were GBP 36,000 and GBP 50,000 plus VAT all-in; no budget for any Mamou-Mani project is public on the pages read.
No public example of a materials-R&D contract with an architecture practice was found; the three-phase, stage-gated skeleton is modelled on UK government R&D procurement and the Lambert agreements.
The skeleton promises no fire class, no outdoor or structural use, no building energy benefit and no service life beyond the cycles run.
lay_summary: We looked at what a London architecture studio that 3D-prints big sculptures from plant-based plastic is working on now, and what a small research deal with them could look like.
They already mix their own plastic recipes, so what we can offer is careful measurements and rules that a computer has checked.
In England, plastic on an indoor wall must pass the same fire tests as any other wall covering, and even a short-lived display still needs a fire safety check.
We wrote a one-page plan with three steps; after each step the studio can stop, and each step has tests that clearly pass or fail.
The plan also lists what we do not promise, such as a fire certificate or that the piece can go outdoors.

glossary.PLA: A plastic made from fermented plant sugar instead of oil.
glossary.PETG: A common clear plastic, here used in recycled form for printing.
glossary.Reaction-to-fire class (Euroclass): A letter grade from A (does not burn) to F for how much a material feeds a fire; s is for smoke and d for burning drips.
glossary.C-s3, d2: A middle fire grade with no limit on smoke or drips; the guidance level for wall and ceiling surfaces in ordinary rooms in England.
glossary.Lining: The surface material of a wall or ceiling that a fire would touch first.
glossary.Thermoplastic: A plastic that softens and melts when heated.
glossary.TP(a) / TP(b): UK labels for how melting plastics burn; they only apply to things like roof windows and light covers.
glossary.Approved Document B: The English government's guidance on how to meet the fire-safety part of the building rules.
glossary.Fire Safety Order: The 2005 law that makes whoever runs a place assess and manage its fire risks.
glossary.Stage gate: A point between project steps where the client decides whether to pay for the next step.
glossary.Acceptance test: A measurement agreed in advance that decides whether a delivered item passes.
glossary.IP (intellectual property): Legal ownership of ideas, recipes, designs and software.
glossary.Lean: A program that checks every step of a mathematical proof.
glossary.Coupon: A small test piece of material made for measuring.
glossary.Contingency: Money set aside inside a budget for surprises.
glossary.Fab.Pub: The studio's sister workshop that does the large-scale printing.

recommendations: Ask the user to confirm the partner name before anything is sent anywhere.
Decide which entity is the client: the practice (design) or the fabrication arm (materials and printing); the material-intake route sits with the fabrication arm.
Scope the first pilot to an interior, non-structural piece and state the fire position plainly: indicative small-flame screening only, with full classification testing costed in phase 3.

Before using the skeleton, replace its generic 'moisture-responsive element' wording with the actual linker-biology material and re-derive acceptance thresholds A2, B1 and B2 from that material's own frozen predictions.
Re-check the small-flame threshold (150 mm in 60 s) against the regulation annex bytes; it is inherited from an earlier record that flagged a summariser risk.
Have a UK construction lawyer review the IP and liability clauses; the skeleton is not legal advice.
